story: Anchorage funded its police Real Time Crime Center expansion on September 1st, 2026 by an 8 to 4 vote while AO 2026-108, the ordinance governing AI on that camera network, went untouched and returns for public testimony on September 15th, 2026

claims.claim: The Anchorage Assembly voted to spend just under $600,000 expanding the police department's real time crime center.
claims.verbatim: The Assembly voted Tuesday to spend just under $600,000 expanding the police department's real-time crime center, which will give officers centralized access to hundreds of cameras across the city.
claims.notes: Corroborated to the dollar by ADN at $598,998 and to the cent by Must Read Alaska at $598,998.10. See C05 and C06.

claims.claim: The Assembly approved the crime center funding by a vote of 8 to 4.
claims.verbatim: The Assembly ultimately voted 8 to 4 to approve the crime center funding, with East Anchorage's George Martinez joining Scout, McCormick and Volland in opposition.
claims.notes: The same article also renders it as 8-4. Both forms are on the page.

claims.claim: The Assembly took the crime center funding vote on Tuesday September 1st, 2026.
claims.verbatim: The Assembly voted Tuesday to spend just under $600,000 expanding the police department's real-time crime center
claims.notes: Date resolution. The article published Thursday September 3rd and says voted Tuesday, which is September 1st, 2026. Must Read Alaska independently places the approval at the September 1st meeting, and Alaska's News Source reported the AO 2026-108 public hearing was set for the meeting of Sept. 1. A September 3rd vote date is killed.

claims.claim: Four Assembly members voted against the funding, Sydney Scout, Keith McCormick, Daniel Volland and George Martinez.
claims.verbatim: with East Anchorage's George Martinez joining Scout, McCormick and Volland in opposition
claims.notes: Three of the four no votes are the ordinance's own sponsors, which is the deck's structural fact. Cross reads with C14.

claims.claim: The request was for $598,998 funded through federal asset forfeitures, according to a memorandum submitted to the Assembly.
claims.verbatim: The $598,998 requested for the Real Time Crime Center, funded through federal asset forfeitures, would pay for the audio-visual equipment to make the facilities more functional, according to a memorandum submitted to the Assembly in support of the measure.
claims.notes: ADN quoting a municipal memorandum it obtained. The memorandum itself was not reachable, so this is reporting on a primary document and not the document.

claims.claim: Must Read Alaska put the appropriation at $598,998.10.
claims.source_outlet: Must Read Alaska, Marcus Moore, opinion
claims.notes: Opinion column and the only source for the cents. Dollars agree with ADN. If the deck prints the cent figure it must attribute it. Safer alternative for a slide is C05.

claims.claim: Officials say the real time crime center at full capacity could access up to 750 different cameras across the city.
claims.verbatim: At full capacity, officials say the real time crime center would have the ability to access up to 750 different cameras across the city, from police body cameras and drones, to traffic cameras, license plate readers and private security cameras that members of the public give the police permission to use.
claims.notes: 750 is a ceiling, not a deployed count. Never write 750 as cameras now online. See C08.

claims.claim: Chief Sean Case said the Axon package could accommodate as many as 750 feeds at once but that APD has neither the hardware nor the personnel to come close to that.
claims.verbatim: While the technology package purchased through Axon could potentially accommodate as many as 750 different feeds coming in at one time, the Anchorage Police Department has neither the hardware nor personnel to come anywhere close to that, Case said.
claims.notes: The honest counterweight to the 750 headline number. The deck carries it alongside C07.

claims.claim: Anchorage Police Chief Sean Case told the Assembly in August that code is not going to keep up with technology.
claims.value: Code is not going to keep up with technology
claims.verbatim: "Code is not going to keep up with technology," Case told the Assembly in August.
claims.notes: Anchor quote. Confirmed on two separate fetches of the same page. Attribute on the slide to Chief Sean Case via ADN.

claims.claim: Assembly Vice Chair Daniel Volland said he does not think the city needs to be putting the cart before the horse when it comes to potentially sacrificing people's privacy rights.
claims.verbatim: "I find that disturbing. I don't think we need to be putting the cart before the horse when it comes to potentially sacrificing people's privacy rights," Volland said.
claims.notes: Anchor quote, confirmed on two fetches. If the deck trims to the cart clause that is a fair trim, but do not append the two sentences into one without an ellipsis.

claims.claim: Assembly member Sydney Scout said the protections should go into code now so they survive a shift in the political winds.
claims.value: Let's put this into code now
claims.verbatim: Let's put this into code now, so that when power changes, when the political winds shift, as they always do, we have protections for the people, no matter who is overseeing and implementing the system.
claims.notes: Anchor quote and the deck's spine when set against C09. Both speakers use the word code and mean municipal code. Attribute as Scout, quoted by Alaska Public Media.

claims.claim: The privacy ordinance is numbered AO 2026-108.
claims.verbatim: That ordinance — No. AO 2026-108 — will be up for public hearing at the Assembly meeting of Sept. 1.
claims.notes: Corroborated independently by Must Read Alaska, which styles it with a hyphen. Use the Alaska's News Source form, AO 2026-108.

claims.claim: Volland said he and his co sponsors plan to bring the ordinance back before the Assembly on September 15th.
claims.verbatim: Volland said he and his co-sponsors plan on working with the mayor's administration on fine tuning the ordinance, before bringing it back before the Assembly on Sept. 15.
claims.notes: Softening on the forward look only. A stated plan, not a docketed certainty, so write is expected to return or sponsors plan to bring it back. Must Read Alaska separately tells readers they can testify at the September 15th regular meeting or through the city's online form.

claims.claim: The ordinance was proposed by Keith McCormick, Assembly Vice Chair Daniel Volland and North Anchorage member Sydney Scout.
claims.verbatim: McCormick, Assembly Vice Chair Daniel Volland and North Anchorage member Sydney Scout have proposed an ordinance that would codify policies and procedures for the access and storage of information captured by the new surveillance upgrade.
claims.notes: All three sponsors voted against the money. Verified by cross reading C04.

claims.claim: Mayor Suzanne LaFrance's administration told the Assembly the ordinance would unduly limit some core functions of APD operations.
claims.verbatim: The AO before you would unduly limit some core functions of APD operations, including misdemeanor enforcement and joint operations with state and federal partners on illicit drug enforcement.
claims.notes: Softening on attribution. Write the LaFrance administration told the Assembly rather than putting it in the mayor's mouth as words spoken at the podium.

claims.claim: ADN reports the ordinance would prevent the police department from adding artificial intelligence technology with human feature recognition capabilities into the network without Assembly permission.
claims.verbatim: The ordinance would also prevent the police department from adding artificial intelligence technology with human-feature recognition capabilities into the network without Assembly permission.
claims.notes: ATTRIBUTION RULE. The ordinance text was never obtained, so the deck must write ADN reports the ordinance would and never the ordinance would. The most important sentence in the story for an AI deck and it is sourced to reporting only.

claims.claim: Alaska Public Media reports the ordinance would require that data not be shared with federal agencies without a warrant and that the crime center's use of AI be approved by the Assembly.
claims.verbatim: It would also require that data not be shared with federal agencies, like the Department of Homeland Security, without a warrant and that the crime center's use of A.I. be approved by the Assembly.
claims.notes: ATTRIBUTION RULE. Independently corroborates the AI approval provision at C16 from a second newsroom, which is why both survive despite no ordinance text.

claims.claim: ADN reports the technology would be subject to a period of temporary approval and annual reporting requirements.
claims.verbatim: This technology would be subject to a period of 'temporary approval' and annual reporting requirements.
claims.notes: ATTRIBUTION RULE. Single sourced to ADN, so keep it as a reported detail and do not build a slide's spine on it.

claims.claim: The Assembly last year approved $11.8 million for a new system designed to stream up to 750 camera feeds, automatic license plate readers and drone footage.
claims.verbatim: The Assembly last year approved $11.8 million for a new system designed to stream up to 750 camera feeds, automatic license plate readers and drone footage.
claims.notes: Use $11.8 million on its own, attributed to ADN. The $12.4 million aggregate is killed.

claims.claim: Roughly 216 residents had registered home security cameras as of ADN's August 20th, 2026 report.
claims.verbatim: Roughly 216 residents have registered their home security cameras so far, the newsletter said.
claims.notes: Count carries its own date because the number moves. Note the unit is residents who registered, not cameras, in ADN's phrasing. Do not present 216 and 238 as the same unit without saying so.

claims.claim: There were 238 cameras registered with APD as of Alaska's News Source's August 27th, 2026 report.
claims.verbatim: As of the date of publication, there are 238 cameras registered with APD, and the number can be seen through a live dashboard on the APD website.
claims.notes: Count carries its own date. Use the dated reported number, never a present tense count.

claims.claim: Eleven cameras had been integrated with APD as of Alaska's News Source's August 27th, 2026 report.
claims.verbatim: The dashboard also notes that there are 11 cameras that have been integrated with APD.
claims.notes: The gap between 238 registered and 11 integrated is the most useful pair of numbers in the story and both come from one page on one date. Registered means APD knows the camera exists. Integrated means APD can pull the feed. Keep the distinction on the slide.

claims.claim: ADN reported the crime center launched in September with one employee and about 15 cameras located at APD properties and Town Square Park.
claims.verbatim: When it launched in September, the center operated on a small scale, with one employee and about 15 cameras located at APD properties and Town Square Park.
claims.notes: SOFTENING ON THE YEAR. ADN writes in September with no year and the deck must not supply one. Write at launch or when it launched in September. The figure is the growth baseline against 238 registered.

claims.claim: The Assembly considered a $600,000 contract with ThunderCat Technology to buy new equipment for the Real Time Crime Center on Elmore Road.
claims.verbatim: Earlier this month, the Anchorage Assembly considered a $600,000 contract with a company called ThunderCat Technology to purchase new equipment for the police department's relatively new Real-Time Crime Center on Elmore Road.
claims.notes: ThunderCat is the vendor on the equipment contract, Axon is the platform vendor. Do not merge the two.

claims.claim: APD's own Safe Anchorage page states that all scanned license plate reader data is automatically deleted after 14 days.
claims.verbatim: All scanned data is automatically deleted after 14 days
claims.notes: PRIMARY. The department's own published page, fetched today. Independently confirms ADN's reporting. Page is undated, so date_of_source is the fetch date.

claims.claim: APD's own Safe Anchorage page states that traffic camera footage is overwritten with new footage every 3 to 5 days.
claims.verbatim: Every 3 to 5 days, this footage is overwritten with new footage
claims.notes: PRIMARY. Corroborated by ADN on August 20th, 2026. Two independent renderings of the same policy, one of them the department's own.

claims.claim: APD's own Safe Anchorage page states that APD does not use Flock cameras.
claims.value: APD does not use Flock cameras
claims.verbatim: APD does not use Flock cameras
claims.notes: PRIMARY, and it is the department's own denial rather than a third party count. Note the scope difference, this covers APD and not the whole state.

claims.claim: APD's own Safe Anchorage page states that municipal use of facial recognition technology was officially banned by the Anchorage Assembly in 2023.
claims.verbatim: municipal use of facial recognition technology was officially banned by the Anchorage Assembly in 2023
claims.notes: PRIMARY and LOAD BEARING. A 2023 ban already covers facial recognition, so AO 2026-108's AI provision at C16 is about the wider category of human feature recognition and about Assembly consent before anything new is attached. THE DECK MUST NOT WRITE THAT AI IS CURRENTLY UNREGULATED IN ANCHORAGE.

claims.claim: ADN reported, citing The New York Times, that there are around 120,000 Flock cameras spread over every state in the country except Alaska.
claims.verbatim: According to reporting by The New York Times, there are around 120,000 Flock cameras spread over every state in the country except one: Alaska
claims.notes: SOFTENING, this is third hand. ADN citing the NYT. Write around 120,000 nationwide, according to New York Times reporting cited by ADN. deflock.org returns HTTP 403 to an automated fetch so no primary was reachable.

claims.claim: ADN reported that data from DeFlock, an open source project tracking automated license plate readers, does not show any such mounted cameras in Alaska.
claims.verbatim: Data from DeFlock, an open-source project tracking automated license plate readers around the country, does not show any such mounted cameras in Alaska.
claims.notes: SOFTENING. DeFlock is crowd sourced, so absence of a record is not proof of absence of a camera. Write DeFlock's map shows none in Alaska and not there are none in Alaska. Reinforced by APD's own denial at C27.

claims.claim: Chief Case said detectives are using artificial intelligence systems similar to commercial large language models to manage case files and query them more efficiently.
claims.verbatim: Detectives in the department are using artificial intelligence systems similar to commercial large language models like ChatGPT and Gemini Notebook to manage case files and query them more efficiently, Case said.
claims.notes: This is the AI already in use, as distinct from the camera network AI that AO 2026-108 would gate. The deck must not blur them. ADN names those products as comparisons, not as what APD runs.

claims.claim: ADN reported that Anchorage businesses, particularly big box retailers, have started sharing shoplifting data among themselves and with APD through a platform called Auror.
claims.verbatim: A number of businesses in Anchorage, particularly big box retailers, have also started sharing data among themselves and with APD on shoplifting through a platform called Auror.
claims.notes: A private sector channel outside the crime center contract and outside the ordinance as reported. Texture, not a crime center capability.

claims.claim: Alaska Public Media reported that the 750 feeds include more than 250 traffic cameras around the city as well as officer worn cameras and private security cameras.
claims.verbatim: That includes the more than 250 traffic cameras around the city, as well as officer-worn cameras and private security cameras that owners have given police access to.
claims.notes: Magnitude check passes. More than 250 traffic cameras sits inside the 750 ceiling and above the 238 privately registered, so the largest single block is municipal and not private.

claims.claim: Chief Case said cameras can't be pointed into a residence and can't be used without a search warrant that a court allows.
claims.verbatim: None of those cameras can be pointed in those directions. None of those cameras can be used without some sort of search warrant that a court allows us to access that information too.
claims.notes: The preceding sentence sets the context, cameras that look inside property where there is an expectation of privacy. Do not lift the warrant sentence without that context, it is narrower than it sounds alone.

claims.claim: Chief Case said the expenditure is to move the Real Time Crime Center to its final location where it can handle all the staff the department plans to put in there.
claims.verbatim: This expenditure is to move the Real Time Crime Center to its final location where it can handle all the staff that we're planning on putting in there,
claims.notes: What the money buys in the department's own framing. Pairs against C05.

claims.claim: Alaska's News Source reported that a home or business that opts into integration receives a small CORE device from Axon that plugs into the camera.
claims.verbatim: In the case of integration, a home or business opts to receive a 'small CORE device' from Axon that plugs into the camera.
claims.notes: Corroborated at the primary. APD's own Safe Anchorage page describes Level 2 integration through a CORE device.

claims.claim: APD's own Safe Anchorage page describes a voluntary registry in which the owner keeps control at all times and APD must obtain permission to access video.
claims.verbatim: It's a voluntary program and the owner keeps control at all times. APD must obtain permission to access video
claims.notes: PRIMARY. Level 1 is registry only, Level 2 is live integration through the CORE device. The department's own description of the consent model, and it explains the 238 to 11 gap at C21 and C22.

claims.claim: Alaska Landmine reported that APD's director of community relations Gina Romero filed a copyright claim that got a Landmine video critical of Chief Case removed from Facebook.
claims.value: Gina Romero, director of community relations
claims.verbatim: Gina Romero, director of community relations
claims.notes: SOFTENING ON FRAMING. Alaska Landmine is a party to this dispute and is reporting on itself, so it is not disinterested. The video was posted August 28th and the claim filed roughly three days later. Attribute every element to Alaska Landmine.

claims.claim: Gina Romero wrote that after further review APD concluded the Landmine's use may be covered under a valid copyright exception and that APD had contacted Facebook to retract the request.
claims.value: may be covered under a valid copyright exception
claims.verbatim: However, after receiving your message and conducting further review, we have concluded that your use may be covered under a valid copyright exception. We have contacted Facebook accordingly to retract the request.
claims.notes: SOFTENING ON FRAMING only, the quotation is solid. The outlet's own headline calls the strike bogus, which is the outlet's characterization and must not be repeated as fact.

claims.claim: Alaska Landmine reported the video had more than 60,000 views before Facebook took it down.
claims.verbatim: more than 60,000 views
claims.notes: SOFTENING. Self reported traffic from the affected publisher with no independent check. Weakest number in this set, do not put it on a slide as a standalone figure.

claims.claim: Assembly Vice Chair Daniel Volland said he would be curious how the action on social media comports with Constitutional freedom of the press.
claims.verbatim: I guess I'd be interested in knowing more about APD's views regarding the media's rights, or lack thereof, to share excerpts from taxpayer funded recordings of public meetings. I'd also be curious how this action on social media comports with Constitutional freedom of the press.
claims.notes: SOFTENING ON CONTEXT. The quote was given to the outlet that was itself the subject of the takedown. If used, name the outlet in the same breath. Same Volland who sponsored AO 2026-108 and voted no on the money.

stories_surviving: Anchorage funded the Real Time Crime Center expansion 8 to 4 on September 1st, 2026 and did not act on AO 2026-108, which sponsors plan to bring back September 15th, 2026
The gap between what is registered and what is connected, 238 cameras registered and 11 integrated as of August 27th, 2026, against a 750 feed ceiling
AI is already inside APD workflows for case files while the ordinance that would gate AI on the camera network is still unpassed
Alaska is the one state with no Flock cameras on DeFlock's map, and APD says it does not use them

killed.claim: The text of AO 2026-108 itself, including its exact operative language
killed.why: Never obtained. muni.org returns HTTP 403 on every path tried. anchorage.legistar.com/Calendar.aspx loaded but returned only Invalid parameters with no docket data. meetings.muni.org renders a JavaScript search form with no results. Each tried once per the standing repo record. Consequence, every ordinance provision in this file is attributed to reporting and the deck must write ADN reports the ordinance would and never the ordinance would.

killed.claim: Anchorage has spent $12.4 million on police surveillance
killed.why: No verbatim string for the figure was recoverable from the page body, only from the Must Read Alaska headline slug, and the source is an opinion column. It is an advocacy aggregate, not an official municipal total. The arithmetic is sound but it is the checker's addition and not a published fact. Use C19 and C05 separately.

killed.claim: The 8 to 4 vote was taken on September 3rd, 2026
killed.why: Contradicted by the record. Alaska Public Media published Thursday September 3rd and wrote The Assembly voted Tuesday, which is September 1st. Must Read Alaska and Alaska's News Source independently place it at the September 1st meeting. Replaced by C03.

killed.claim: Chief Case said we can't pipe that many camera feeds into the real time crime center for a whole host of reasons
killed.why: Returned on a first fetch but not reproduced on a second targeted fetch of the same page. An anchor quote has to survive re-fetch. The same point is carried safely by C08.

killed.claim: DeFlock's own site reports zero automated license plate readers in Alaska against roughly 120,000 nationwide
killed.why: Could not reach the primary. deflock.me issues a 301 to deflock.org, and both deflock.org and deflock.org/alaska return HTTP 403. Survives only as ADN's characterization at C30.

killed.claim: Must Read Alaska reported the vote tally
killed.why: The tally does not appear in that article. C02 from Alaska Public Media is the sole verified source for 8 to 4.

killed.claim: Mayor Suzanne LaFrance personally testified the ordinance would unduly limit core APD functions
killed.why: Downgraded rather than killed, see C15. The sentence is verified but the speaker attribution was summarized on fetch. Attribute to the LaFrance administration via Alaska Public Media.

killed.claim: A ThunderCat Technology or Axon announcement of the Anchorage award
killed.why: thundercattech.com/news carries no Anchorage announcement. Axon's product page describes the platform generally but names no Anchorage deployment.

killed.claim: The ACLU of Alaska policy director Mike Garvey quote on laws having more permanence
killed.why: Reported by a scout but not present on any page the checker fetched. Not verified, so it does not exist for this deck. The permanence argument is carried instead by Sydney Scout at C11, who is an Assembly member, a sponsor of the ordinance and one of the four no votes.
